column1: Hedonic Prices and Quality Adjusted Price Indices

The thesis titled Hedonic Prices and Quality Adjusted Price Indices Powered by AI by P. Bajari  Z. Cen  V. Chernozhukov  M. Manukonda  S. Vijaykumar  J. Wang  and R. Huerta  J. Li  L. Leng  G. Monokrousos  and S. Wan  presents a novel approach to constructing hedonic price models and quality-adjusted price indices using artificial intelligence (AI). The authors develop empirical models that efficiently process large volumes of unstructured product data  including text  images  prices  and quantities  to produce accurate hedonic price estimates and derived indices. The methodology involves generating abstract product attributes  or features  from descriptions and images using deep neural networks. These attributes are then utilized to estimate the hedonic price function.

The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through its application to Amazon's data for first-party apparel sales  where the authors estimate hedonic prices. The resulting models exhibit high out-of-sample predictive accuracy  with R² values ranging from 80% to 90%. Furthermore  the authors construct an AI-based hedonic Fisher price index  chained at the year-over-year frequency  and compare it with the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and other electronic indices.

The thesis begins by discussing the importance of price indices  such as the CPI  for measuring inflation  consumer welfare  and the cost of living. Traditional methods for constructing price indices  like the Laspeyres and Paasche indices  are reviewed  highlighting their limitations  particularly in dealing with product entry and exit. The authors note that these indices often suffer from selection bias and chain-drift bias due to geometric compounding of measurement errors.

Hedonic price models  introduced by Court (1939) and Griliches (1961)  are presented as a solution to these issues. These models postulate that the prices of differentiated products are determined by the market value of each product's underlying characteristics. By modeling how hedonic prices change while holding product characteristics fixed  economists can measure inflation or deflation. Hedonic prices can be computed for a basket of goods at any time point  addressing the entry/exit problem and reducing chain-drift biases by making long or low-frequency comparisons.

The authors propose an alternative approach to building hedonic models using electronic data and AI. This method automatically generates product characteristics  which are used to predict prices accurately. The approach is scalable and cost-effective compared to traditional methods  which rely on human expertise and extensive field surveys. The authors emphasize the potential of leveraging electronic records to improve the construction of price indices  a topic of significant interest to both academic researchers and statistical agencies.

The thesis concludes by highlighting the success of the AI-powered hedonic models in approximating real-world prices and accurately estimating the hedonic price function. The authors express gratitude to various contributors and acknowledge the support received during the project's development. The paper was first publicly circulated in 2021 as a CEMMAP Working Paper CWP04/21 and is available on arXiv.
